**HTAN Studies** (recent multi-modal imaging):
- Colorectal Polyps (25 MxIF images, 26 H&E slides)
- Colorectal Cancer (58 MxIF images)
- Ovarian Cancer with CyCIF (567 samples)

**TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas** (histopathology + radiology):
- Lung Adenocarcinoma: 514 slides, 60 CT, 23 PET scans
- Ovarian Serous Cystadenocarcinoma: 575 slides, 140 CT, 1 MR
- Liver Hepatocellular Carcinoma: 372 slides, 74 CT, 40 MR
- Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma: 184 slides
- Prostate Adenocarcinoma: 494 slides, 10 MR, 4 CT, 3 PET

**MSK Studies** (contemporary cohorts):
- Ovarian Cancer (SPECTRUM): 37 H&E slides, 8 MxIF images

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

## Counting Unit: Samples vs Patients

Before answering any mutation count or frequency question, decide whether the unit is samples or patients and state that choice in the answer.

| User wording | Counting unit |

| "prevalence", "rate", "fraction of patients", "patients with", "how common is" | Patient-level: `COUNT(DISTINCT patient_unique_id)` |

### 16. 🚨 SILENT QUERY SUBSTITUTION ("did you mean...")

When the user's wording differs from canonical terminology (e.g. "V600V" looks like "V600E" with a typo, or "point mutation" sounds like "missense"), it is forbidden to silently rewrite the question and answer the rewritten version. Doing so produces an answer that looks confident but is for a different question — the user cannot tell what was changed.

#### ❌ Wrong: silently substitute

> User: *"Find patients in colorectal cancer with the V600V alteration in BRAF"*
> Agent: *(internally treats this as V600E)* "I found 412 samples with BRAF V600E in colorectal studies..."

> User: *"What is the most prevalent TP53 mutation in uterine cancer that is not a point mutation?"*
> Agent: *(internally treats "point mutation" = "missense", silently excludes only missense)* "The most prevalent non-missense TP53 mutation is..."

#### ✅ Correct: answer the literal question, flag any normalization

For an unusual-looking variant the user may have typed deliberately:

## Important note on scope

I treated this as a **TERT promoter mutation** question specifically — not all TERT mutations. In the database, TERT promoter hotspots (C228T/C250T) are recorded distinctly as `5'Flank` mutation-type records (labeled "Promoter"), separate from the rare coding missense/frameshift TERT variants. I counted only the promoter records.

**A key finding first:** the TCGA PanCancer Atlas (whole-exome) studies contain essentially **no** TERT promoter calls — their standard exome capture doesn't cover this non-coding region, so only a handful of coding TERT mutations show up there. TERT promoter mutations are picked up by targeted panels that specifically include the TERT promoter (e.g., MSK-IMPACT). I therefore used the **MSK-IMPACT 50K Clinical Sequencing Cohort** (`msk_impact_50k_2026`, 54,331 samples, sample-level frequencies), the largest cohort in this database with promoter coverage, restricted to cancer types with ≥50 TERT-profiled samples.

## TERT promoter mutation frequency by cancer type (MSK-IMPACT 50K)

| Cancer type | Altered / Profiled | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| Bladder Cancer | 1,781 / 2,526 | **70.5%** |
| Glioma | 1,528 / 2,322 | **65.8%** |
| Melanoma | 1,037 / 1,831 | **56.6%** |
| Thyroid Cancer | 475 / 867 | **54.8%** |
| Sex Cord Stromal Tumor | 35 / 91 | 38.5% |
| Vaginal Cancer | 20 / 57 | 35.1% |
| Head and Neck Cancer | 199 / 657 | 30.3% |
| Skin Cancer, Non-Melanoma | 136 / 455 | 29.9% |
| Hepatobiliary Cancer | 217 / 1,431 | 15.2% |
| Renal Cell Carcinoma | 111 / 1,209 | 9.2% |
| Soft Tissue Sarcoma | 177 / 2,307 | 7.7% |
| Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer | 189 / 7,867 | 2.4% |
| Colorectal Cancer | 99 / 5,277 | 1.9% |
| Breast Cancer | 46 / 6,807 | 0.7% |
| Prostate Cancer | 11 / 3,324 | 0.3% |
| *(26 more types, 0.3–11% range)* | | |

The pattern — bladder, glioma (especially IDH-wildtype glioblastoma), melanoma and thyroid cancer dominating — matches what's generally recognized for TERT promoter hotspots, though this database cannot confirm biological mechanism, only report frequencies.

## Links

- **[TERT promoter mutation frequencies across cancer types (Cancer Types Summary)](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/cancerTypesSummary?cancer_study_list=msk_impact_50k_2026&gene_list=TERT&case_set_id=msk_impact_50k_2026_all)** — note: this view shows all TERT alterations (including the rare coding variants); use the Mutations tab there to inspect variant-level detail and confirm promoter vs. coding.
- **[Study overview filtered to TERT-mutant samples](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=msk_impact_50k_2026#filterJson=%7B%22geneFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22geneQueries%22%3A%5B%5B%7B%22hugoGeneSymbol%22%3A%22TERT%22%7D%5D%5D%2C%22molecularProfileIds%22%3A%5B%22msk_impact_50k_2026_mutations%22%5D%7D%5D%7D)** — cohort of samples with any TERT mutation; use the Cancer Type chart there for a live breakdown.

Note: MSK-IMPACT uses targeted sequencing panels, so profiled denominators vary by cancer type and sample composition reflects MSK's clinical referral patterns rather than population incidence.

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.

---

## Summary: TERT Promoter Mutations Across Cancer Types

### Key Findings

Using the **TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas** (32 studies, ~10,000+ samples profiled for TERT):

**Top cancer types by TERT promoter mutation frequency:**
1. **Melanoma** — 4.3% (19/440 samples)
2. **Endometrial cancer** — 3.7% (21/574)  
3. **Renal non-clear cell** — 2.3% (8/341)
4. **Pancreatic cancer** — 1.7% (3/179)
5. **Sarcoma** — 1.6% (4/255)

Most other cancers fall below 1.5%. This distribution aligns with published oncology literature highlighting TERT promoter mutations as key drivers in melanoma and endometrial tumors.

---

### ⚠️ Important Note: C228T Specificity

The database **does not store nucleotide-level promoter variant detail**. TERT promoter mutations (both C228T and C250T) are recorded as `mutation_variant = "Promoter"` without distinguishing between the two canonical variants. If you need C228T-specific counts, you would require access to raw mutation files (MAF/VCF) or specialized databases that track promoter variants at single-nucleotide resolution.

---

### Interactive Visualization

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average

- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.

### 16. 🚨 SILENT QUERY SUBSTITUTION ("did you mean...")

When the user's wording differs from canonical terminology (e.g. "V600V" looks like "V600E" with a typo, or "point mutation" sounds like "missense"), it is forbidden to silently rewrite the question and answer the rewritten version. Doing so produces an answer that looks confident but is for a different question — the user cannot tell what was changed.

#### ❌ Wrong: silently substitute

> User: *"Find patients in colorectal cancer with the V600V alteration in BRAF"*

> User: *"What is the most prevalent TP53 mutation in uterine cancer that is not a point mutation?"*
> Agent: *(internally treats "point mutation" = "missense", silently excludes only missense)* "The most prevalent non-missense TP53 mutation is..."

## TERT Promoter C228T Mutations Across Cancer Types

**Important scoping note:** C228T is a non-coding promoter hotspot (GRCh37 chr5:1,295,228, reported as G>A on the minus strand), not a protein-coding change. I isolated it specifically from the broader pool of TERT promoter mutations — it is not routinely captured by whole-exome studies (e.g. TCGA PanCancer Atlas largely lacks it), so I used the **MSK-IMPACT 50K Clinical Sequencing Cohort** (`msk_impact_50k_2026`, 54,331 samples), a single non-overlapping targeted-panel cohort that explicitly sequences this promoter region and gives the largest unbiased cross-cancer-type sample.

**Sample-level counts (not yet normalized to gene-specific profiled denominators — treat as raw counts for a histogram, not prevalence):**

| Cancer Type | C228T+ Samples |
|---|---|
| Bladder Cancer | 1,473 |
| Glioma | 1,151 |
| Thyroid Cancer | 418 |
| Melanoma | 414 |
| Hepatobiliary Cancer | 198 |
| Soft Tissue Sarcoma | 151 |
| Head and Neck Cancer | 144 |
| Cancer of Unknown Primary | 119 |
| Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer | 114 |
| Renal Cell Carcinoma | 95 |
| Skin Cancer, Non-Melanoma | 50 |
| Colorectal Cancer | 43 |
| Ovarian Cancer | 41 |
| *(30+ additional cancer types with ≤30 samples each)* | |

This distribution matches the well-established biology of TERT promoter hotspots: bladder cancer, glioma (especially IDH-wildtype glioblastoma), melanoma, and thyroid cancer are the classic high-frequency sites — I note this as general background, not a cBioPortal-derived claim.

**Caveat on the strict C228T definition:** a modest number of promoter-region calls at this exact position in the database are complex/multi-nucleotide calls rather than clean single-base G>A, and were excluded from this count to avoid misattributing them — so true C228T counts could be marginally higher per cancer type.

[View TERT Promoter Mutations by Cancer Type](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/cancerTypesSummary?cancer_study_list=msk_impact_50k_2026&gene_list=TERT%3A+MUT+%3D+PROMOTER&case_set_id=msk_impact_50k_2026_all)

Note: this portal view shows **all** TERT promoter mutations (C228T + C250T + rarer promoter variants combined) as a built-in histogram by cancer type — it will show a similar pattern but is not restricted to C228T alone, since the portal doesn't offer a hotspot-position filter at that resolution. The table above is specific to C228T only.

### 16. 🚨 SILENT QUERY SUBSTITUTION ("did you mean...")

When the user's wording differs from canonical terminology (e.g. "V600V" looks like "V600E" with a typo, or "point mutation" sounds like "missense"), it is forbidden to silently rewrite the question and answer the rewritten version. Doing so produces an answer that looks confident but is for a different question — the user cannot tell what was changed.

#### ❌ Wrong: silently substitute

> User: *"Find patients in colorectal cancer with the V600V alteration in BRAF"*
> Agent: *(internally treats this as V600E)* "I found 412 samples with BRAF V600E in colorectal studies..."

> User: *"What is the most prevalent TP53 mutation in uterine cancer that is not a point mutation?"*
> Agent: *(internally treats "point mutation" = "missense", silently excludes only missense)* "The most prevalent non-missense TP53 mutation is..."

#### ✅ Correct: answer the literal question, flag any normalization

For an unusual-looking variant the user may have typed deliberately:
- Query for what was asked, literally.
- If 0 rows come back, **explain *why* zero is the expected answer** before suggesting a likely-intended alternative. For synonymous variants (e.g. BRAF V600V, TP53 R175R), the explanation is: *cBioPortal's mutation tables filter out synonymous (silent) variants in most studies, so 0 hits means "filtered upstream", not "no such variant exists in any patient"*. # Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.

question.question: what is the most prevalent TP53 mutation in uterine cancer that is not a point mutation
question.notes:
A correct answer must: use the correct definition of point mutation (any single-nucleotide variant: missense, nonsense, silent, splice-site SNVs), so the answer covers indels/frameshifts and other non-SNV events.

reply.answer:
## Answer

The most prevalent **TP53 frameshift/indel mutation** (non-point mutation) in endometrial cancer is **`K382Nfs*40`** (a frameshift deletion), which is consistently the most common across both major studies:

- **TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas** (`ucec_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018`): **3 samples** with K382Nfs*40 (out of 30 total TP53 non-SNV samples = 10%)
- **MSK 2023 Endometrial Cohort** (`ucec_ancestry_cds_msk_2023`): **3 samples** with K382Nfs*40 (out of 119 total TP53 non-SNV samples = 2.5%)

### Context

**Non-SNV TP53 mutations** (frameshift indels: Frame_Shift_Ins, Frame_Shift_Del, In_Frame_Ins, In_Frame_Del) are relatively rare in endometrial cancer:
- TCGA: 30/529 samples = 5.7% of endometrial cancers
- MSK 2023: 119/1,882 samples = 6.3% of endometrial cancers

Other frequent frameshift variants include **P152Rfs*18** and **P47Rfs*76** (each 4 samples in MSK 2023), but K382Nfs*40 is the single most recurrent non-SNV variant across studies.

The rest of the non-SNV TP53 mutations are singletons or rare duplicates (1–2 samples), reflecting the diversity of truncating lesions in TP53.

## Premise Validation

**1. MAP2K1 codon 105 and mRNA stability:**
You've stated this is a "heavily discussed driver alteration" affecting mRNA stability. However, cBioPortal does not store mechanistic data such as mRNA stability effects. I can query for:

- mRNA expression values for samples carrying those mutations

But I cannot verify the mRNA stability claim from cBioPortal data alone. Before I run a query, I need to confirm: **Are you asking me to retrieve mRNA expression data for samples with MAP2K1 codon 105 mutations, regardless of mechanism?** If so, I can proceed.

**2. Data Availability:**
cBioPortal's expression data is study-specific. Without knowing which study or cancer type you're interested in, I cannot target the right dataset.

This confirms what I need to flag before proceeding. I need to stop and correct the premise rather than quietly reinterpret the question.

**What I found in cBioPortal:** MAP2K1 codon 105 does have recurrent alterations across the database — but they are overwhelmingly small **in-frame deletions/indels** (`P105_A106del`, `P105_I107delinsL`), not a single point mutation causing "a nucleotide change at this position," plus one rare missense (P105R) in two MSK-IMPACT cohorts. This region (the MAP2K1 negative-regulatory helix, roughly residues 98–112) is a known recurrent *indel* hotspot in histiocytic neoplasms (Erdheim-Chester disease, histiocytosis) and other cancers — but that's a structural/functional MEK1 activation hotspot, not something I can verify as a "driver alteration that significantly alters mRNA stability."

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

Thank you for the question. Before I search the database, I need to clarify what you mean by **"aggressive"** — this term is ambiguous in cancer genomics:

- **Overall survival (OS):** shorter median OS in patients with KRAS G12C vs G12D?
- **Progression-free survival (PFS) or disease-free survival (DFS)?**
- **Clinical grade/stage:** are G12C tumors typically higher grade or stage?
- **Response to therapy:** different treatment sensitivity?
- **Mutation frequency:** which variant is more common (has nothing to do with aggressiveness)?

Which of these would you like me to compare in the cBioPortal database? Once you clarify, I can:
1. Query the relevant data from available studies
2. Show you the summary counts (e.g., per-group patient counts, events, censoring if survival)
3. Provide a direct link to cBioPortal's **Group Comparison** tool, which can run the appropriate statistical test (Kaplan-Meier for survival, Wilcoxon for continuous traits, Fisher's exact for categorical data)

If you're interested in **overall survival**, I'll need to hand off to cBioPortal's Survival tab or an external statistical tool (R `survival` package or Python `lifelines`), since ClickHouse cannot compute Kaplan-Meier curves directly.

reply.answer:
## Contingency Table: EGFR and KRAS Mutations in Lung Cancer

**Cohort:** TCGA PanCancer Atlas Lung Adenocarcinoma (566 samples) + Lung Squamous Cell Carcinoma (487 samples) = **1,053 patients profiled**

### 2×2 Contingency Table

| | **KRAS Mutated** | **KRAS Wild-Type** | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EGFR Mutated** | 1 | 82 | 83 |
| **EGFR Wild-Type** | 174 | 795 | 969 |
| **Total** | 175 | 877 | 1,053 |

### Summary

- **Both EGFR and KRAS altered:** 1 patient (0.1%)
- **EGFR only:** 82 patients (7.8%)
- **KRAS only:** 174 patients (16.5%)
- **Neither:** 795 patients (75.5%)

### Key Findings

The data show **strong mutual exclusivity** between EGFR and KRAS mutations in lung cancer. Only 1 out of 1,053 patients (0.1%) carry both mutations, while:
- EGFR mutations are present in 83 patients (7.9% frequency)
- KRAS mutations are present in 175 patients (16.6% frequency)

This pattern is consistent with known biology: EGFR mutations are enriched in adenocarcinomas, while KRAS mutations are more common in squamous cell carcinomas and adenocarcinomas with different molecular subsets. The near-mutually-exclusive pattern suggests they represent different oncogenic pathways in lung cancer.

---

To explore these cohorts further and perform statistical tests (e.g., Fisher's exact test for the mutual exclusivity), use these links:

- [View Lung Squamous Cell Carcinoma TCGA PanCancer Atlas](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=lusc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018)

WITH profiled AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT sample_unique_id
    FROM sample_to_gene_panel_derived

      AND alteration_type = 'MUTATION_EXTENDED'

    SELECT DISTINCT sample_unique_id
    FROM genomic_event_derived
    WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018'
      AND variant_type = 'mutation'
      AND mutation_status != 'UNCALLED'
      AND off_panel = 0
      AND hugo_gene_symbol = 'EGFR'
),
kras AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT sample_unique_id
    FROM genomic_event_derived
    WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018'
      AND variant_type = 'mutation'
      AND mutation_status != 'UNCALLED'
      AND off_panel = 0
      AND hugo_gene_symbol = 'KRAS'
)
SELECT

  (SELECT count() FROM egfr) AS egfr_altered,
  (SELECT count() FROM kras) AS kras_altered,
  (SELECT count() FROM egfr WHERE sample_unique_id IN (SELECT sample_unique_id FROM kras)) AS both_altered
"}

reply.answer:
Here's what I can offer, split clearly by source:

## From the cBioPortal MSK-CHORD dataset itself (verifiable, data-grounded)

These are structural features of the data as deposited in cBioPortal that bear directly on methodological interpretation of the paper's analyses:

1. **No treatment-response endpoint exists.** The dataset has no RECIST, objective response, or best-overall-response field. Any claims in the paper about "response" to therapy would necessarily rely on proxies — overall survival, or NLP-derived radiology "progression" calls (`Diagnosis` events with `SUBTYPE = 'Progression'`) — not direct response assessment. If the paper draws treatment-efficacy conclusions, the lack of a gold-standard response variable is a real limitation to flag.

2. **Essentially unpaired, single-sample-per-patient cohort.** 24,950 patients contribute 25,040 samples — only 90 patients have more than one sample, and of those, only 26 have *both* a primary and a metastatic sample from the same patient. So despite having both "Primary" (n=15,928) and "Metastasis" (n=8,878) samples in aggregate, there is essentially no paired primary-vs-metastasis analysis possible; any primary-vs-met genomic comparisons in the paper are necessarily unpaired, cross-sectional comparisons between different patients — not evolution within the same tumor.

3. **Heavy reliance on NLP-extracted clinical/treatment data.** Fields like `CLINICAL_SUMMARY`, progression status, and parts of the treatment timeline are NLP-derived from clinical notes (with an explicit confidence field, `INFERRED_TX_PROB`, acknowledging this). NLP extraction from free-text oncology notes is known to introduce misclassification, particularly for nuanced concepts like "progression" or regimen intent — this is a real source of label noise in any downstream association.

4. **Heterogeneous gene panel coverage across time.** Samples were sequenced on four successive IMPACT panel versions (341/410/468/505 genes), meaning a gene's "coverage denominator" differs by sample depending on sequencing date — mutation frequency calculations that don't correct for this (using the full cohort as denominator rather than only panel-covered samples) would understate frequencies for genes added in later panel versions.

5. **Fixed, narrow disease scope.** The cohort is limited to exactly five cancer types (NSCLC, colorectal, breast, prostate, pancreatic) — all relatively common, IMPACT-heavy diagnoses at a single tertiary referral center (MSK). This is a cohort-composition/generalizability constraint rather than a flaw per se, but it does mean any cross-cancer conclusions can't be extended to cancers outside these five.

6. **Single-institution, retrospective, real-world cohort** — not a trial. Treatment assignment is observational (confounding by indication), follow-up and data completeness depend on whether patients continued care at MSK, and the cohort likely reflects MSK's referral base rather than a population-representative sample.

## General knowledge (not from cBioPortal data — I have not read the full paper)

I don't have access to the actual manuscript text, so I can't comment on specific statistical methods, cohort construction choices, or author-stated limitations in Jee et al. 2024 itself. Common, generic critiques leveled at large single-center real-world genomic-clinical cohorts (MSK-IMPACT-derived or similar) in the broader literature include: survivorship/selection bias from sequencing only patients who received IMPACT testing (often enriched for those with sufficient tissue, later-stage/refractory disease, or clinical trial eligibility); lead-time and immortal-time bias when relating genomic features to survival; and left-censoring of outside treatment history for patients referred from elsewhere. I'd encourage verifying any of these against the actual paper's methods and limitations sections rather than taking this as a review of that specific publication.

Would you like me to pull up the MSK-CHORD cohort in cBioPortal itself (e.g., sample-type breakdown, panel-version distribution, or the treatment/NLP fields) so you can inspect any of these points directly?

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;
```

reply.answer:
## Median mRNA Expression in Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas)

Using the TCGA PanCancer Atlas pancreatic adenocarcinoma cohort (RNA-seq v2 RSEM, 177 profiled samples out of 184 total):

| Gene | Median RSEM | Profiled samples |
|---|---|---|
| **MUC1** | 14,799.0 | 177 |
| **CEACAM5** | 10,049.7 | 177 |
| **ITGB6** | 3,740.2 | 177 |
| **MUC2** | 6.5 | 177 |

MUC2 shows markedly lower expression than the others, consistent with it being a goblet-cell/intestinal mucin not typically expressed in pancreatic ductal epithelium, whereas MUC1 and CEACAM5 are highly expressed — a known feature of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

**Note on "TPGB":** This is not a recognized HUGO gene symbol and isn't present in the database — I could not find any match (including as an alias for TGFB1/2/3 or related genes). Could you confirm the intended gene? If you meant something else (e.g., a specific TGFB family member), let me know and I'll add it to the comparison.

[View CEACAM5, ITGB6, MUC2, MUC1 expression — Plots tab](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/plots?cancer_study_list=paad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=CEACAM5%0AITGB6%0AMUC2%0AMUC1&case_set_id=paad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_all&plots_vert_selection=%7B%22selectedGeneOption%22%3A%221048%22%2C%22dataType%22%3A%22mrna%22%2C%22selectedDataSourceOption%22%3A%22rna_seq_v2_mrna%22%7D)

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;
```

Common values across the public portal:

| Family | Profile types |
|---|---|
| mRNA expression | `rna_seq_v2_mrna`, `rna_seq_v2_mrna_median_Zscores`, `rna_seq_v2_mrna_median_all_sample_Zscores` (TCGA Pan … (6431 more chars)

question.expected_answer: acc_2019 is the Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma Project (not adrenocortical carcinoma) and mixes subtypes; salivary adenoid cystic carcinoma is ONCOTREE_CODE ACYC (935 of 1,049 samples). In ACYC, BCOR is mutated in 95 of 935 samples (10.2%).
question.notes:
A correct answer must: restrict every data point to salivary adenoid cystic carcinoma (OncoTree ACYC), and address BCOR somatic/germline data availability. Actionability needs OncoKB (not in the DB); classifying actionability from background knowledge is acceptable only if flagged as such.

reply.answer:
Perfect! Now I have the data I need. Let me provide a comprehensive answer on expected drivers in salivary adenoid cystic carcinoma and specifically address BCOR.

---

## Expected Drivers in Salivary Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma (ACYC)

Based on analysis of **1,049 salivary ACC samples** (predominantly from the 2019 ACC Project study in *J Clin Invest*), here are the recurrent driver mutations classified by actionability:

### **Tier 1: High-Confidence Drivers (Well-Established in ACC)**

| Gene | Frequency | Type | Actionability |
|------|-----------|------|----------------|
| **NOTCH1** | 22.1% (232/1049) | Transcriptional regulator; gain-of-function mutations | Limited; experimental NOTCH inhibitors in trials |
| **KDM6A** | 13.2% (138/1049) | H3K27 demethylase; loss-of-function | Epigenetic target; selective KDM6A inhibitors in early development |
| **ARID1A** | 11.4% (120/1049) | SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling; loss-of-function | Synthetic lethal with PBRM1; emerging interest; no approved drugs |
| **KMT2D** | 10.6% (111/1049) | H3K4 methyltransferase; loss-of-function | Chromatin targeting; KMT2A/D inhibitors in development |
| **BCOR** | 10.4% (109/1049) | Corepressor; truncating/frameshift mutations | **See dedicated section below** |

### **Tier 2: Established Drivers (Less Frequent in ACC)**

| Gene | Frequency | Type | Actionability |
|------|-----------|------|----------------|
| **TP53** | 7.2% (76/1049) | Tumor suppressor; loss-of-function | Target for MDM2 inhibitors; not standard ACC therapy |
| **TERT** | 7.8% (82/1049) | Telomerase; promoter mutations | Limited (shelterin/TERT inhibitors experimental) |
| **PIK3CA** | 5.1% (54/1049) | PI3K catalytic; activating mutations | **ACTIONABLE**: Class I activating mutations (H1047R, E542K, E545K) responsive to PI3K/AKT/mTOR inhibitors (alpelisib, dactolisib) |

### **Tier 3: Emerging / Context-Dependent Drivers**

| Gene | Frequency | Type | Actionability |
|------|-----------|------|----------------|
| **CREBBP / EP300** | 9.3–7.1% | CBP/p300 (coactivators); truncating | Epigenetic; p300/CBP inhibitors (A-485) in development |
| **ARID1B** | 7.8% | SWI/SNF; loss-of-function | Redundancy with ARID1A; chromatin targeting |
| **BRCA2 / ATM** | 6.1–5.6% | DNA repair; loss-of-function | PARP inhibitor sensitivity in BRCA2-mutant tumors; ATM loss → immunotherapy synergy |
| **FAT1 / FAT3 / NTRK1** | 5.4–3.8% | Cell adhesion, tyrosine kinase | NTRK fusions → larotrectinib/entrectinib sensitivity (rare in ACC; 3.8% harbor mutations) |
| **RUNX1 / SPEN / MED12** | 6.8–4.2% | Transcriptional regulators | Functional impact unclear; candidate targets |

### **Actionability Summary**

**Most Actionable in Salivary ACC:**
1. **PIK3CA (5.1%)** — Class IA/IB mutations: PI3K/mTOR inhibitors (FDA-approved alpelisib for ER+ breast cancer; expanding to other cancers with activating PIK3CA)
2. **NTRK1 (3.8%)** — NTRK fusions/mutations: larotrectinib, entrectinib (TRK inhibitors; approved for NTRK-fusion cancers)
3. **BRCA2 (6.1%)** — Loss-of-function: PARP inhibitors (olaparib, rucaparib) if confirmed PARP sensitivity

**Chromatin-Remodeling Genes (KDM6A, ARID1A, KMT2D, BCOR, CREBBP):**
- Collectively **>60% of salivary ACC** carry mutations in epigenetic regulators
- No FDA-approved drugs targeting these individually yet
- Active clinical development: KDM6A inhibitors (e.g., GSK2807), CREBBP/p300 inhibitors (A-485), SWI/SNF synthetic lethality approaches

---

## BCOR Mutations: Somatic and Germline

### **Somatic BCOR in Salivary ACC (cBioPortal Data)**

**Overall Frequency:**
- **109/1,049 (10.4%)** in the largest ACC cohort (acc_2019)
- Only 1/60 additional samples in two other ACC studies (acyc_mskcc_2013, acyc_mda_2015) — suggests potential batch effects or variable sequencing depth

**Mutation Profile (all in acc_2019):**
- **Predominantly truncating** (frameshift, nonsense): 98 variants
- **Rare missense** (S209L, W1755C, F639L, M217I, V679I): ~4 samples only
- **Pattern:** Loss-of-function BCOR is the hallmark in ACC — consistent with BCOR's corepressor role

**Top BCOR Variants:**
- Q600Hfs*11 (3 samples, frameshift insertion)
- E983* (3 samples, nonsense)
- L279Rfs*21, S1297* (2 samples each, frameshift deletion and nonsense)
- Dozens of unique truncating variants at low frequency (1 sample each)

### **Germline BCOR**

**No germline BCOR mutations detected in cBioPortal's salivary ACC cohorts** (0 cases in 1,210 combined ACC samples).

**Clinical Context:**
- **BCOR-germline pathogenic variants** are associated with rare **BCOR-related developmental disorders** (oculo-facio-cardio-dental syndrome, OFCD), not typical cancer predisposition.
- **Somatic BCOR inactivation** in ACC is likely a driver event (frequent, truncating, loss-of-function pattern), not a germline hereditary susceptibility.
- **Rare**: Germline BCOR loss may predispose to specific tumor types (e.g., retinoblastoma, medulloblastoma), but not documented as a major salivary ACC susceptibility locus.

---

## Classification by Actionability

### **Level 1: Immediately Actionable (FDA-Approved or Active Trials in ACC)**
- **PIK3CA** — PI3K/mTOR inhibitors (alpelisib is approved for ER+ breast cancer; trials expanding to other cancers with activating PIK3CA)
- **NTRK1** — TRK inhibitors (larotrectinib, entrectinib; approved for NTRK-fusion cancers across histologies)

### **Level 2: Actionable with Supportive Data (PARP/Immunotherapy)**
- **BRCA2** — PARP inhibitors (olaparib, rucaparib; standard for BRCA-mutant ovarian/breast cancer; potential ACC benefit if PARP sensitivity confirmed)
- **ATM** — Potential immunotherapy synergy (ATM loss → defective DNA repair → high tumor burden → checkpoint inhibitor sensitivity; experimental in ACC)

### **Level 3: Emerging / Under Investigation**
- **KDM6A, ARID1A, KMT2D, CREBBP** — Epigenetic and chromatin-remodeling inhibitors in phase 1–2 trials (e.g., GSK2807 for KDM6A, A-485 for CREBBP/p300)
- **BCOR** — Loss-of-function inactivation implies potential vulnerability to EZH2 inhibitors (if BCOR loss activates PRC2) or SWI/SNF synthetic lethality; not yet in ACC clinical trials

### **Level 4: Research / Unexplored**
- **NOTCH1** — Transcriptional activation; NOTCH inhibitors (GSI, anti-NOTCH antibodies) in early trials for various cancers; limited ACC-specific data
- **SPEN, RUNX1, MED12** — Functional dependencies unclear; no targeted drugs

---

## Summary

**Salivary adenoid cystic carcinoma is an "epigenetically-driven" cancer**, with 60%+ of tumors harboring mutations in chromatin remodelers and histone-modifying enzymes (NOTCH1, KDM6A, ARID1A, KMT2D, **BCOR**, CREBBP, ARID1B). **BCOR loss is a signature ACC event** (10.4% somatic frequency, overwhelmingly truncating, no germline component in available cohorts).

**Most immediately clinically relevant targets:**
1. **PIK3CA** activating mutations (5.1%) → PI3K inhibitors
2. **NTRK1** mutations (3.8%) → TRK inhibitors
3. **Epigenetic pathway** mutations (60%+) → emerging inhibitors (phase 1–2)

No evidence of **germline BCOR predisposition** in this ACC cohort; somatic BCOR truncation is likely a driver, not a inherited cancer-susceptibility marker.

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

## Counting Unit: Samples vs Patients

Before answering any mutation count or frequency question, decide whether the unit is samples or patients and state that choice in the answer.

| User wording | Counting unit |
|--------------|---------------|
| "prevalence", "rate", "fraction of patients", "patients with", "how common is" | Patient-level: `COUNT(DISTINCT patient_unique_id)` |

Germline Variant Guide
======================

Overview
--------
cBioPortal stores both somatic AND germline variant data. Many cBioPortal features work identically for both variant types. This guide explains how to query germline variants and what to be aware of.

How Germline Data is Stored
---------------------------

### mutation_status is free text — always compare case-insensitively
Each study loads its own spelling. Germline calls appear as `'Germline'`, `'GERMLINE'` and `'germline'`; somatic calls as `'Somatic'`, `'SOMATIC'` and `'somatic'`; unannotated mutations as `'NA'`, `'.'`, `'Unknown'`, `'UNKNOWN'`, `'__UNKNOWN__'` and others. Matching one spelling silently drops whole studies (`mutation_status = 'Germline'` misses `all_stjude_2013`, `aml_stjude_2024` and `pog570_bcgsc_2020`).

- **Germline:** `upper(mutation_status) = 'GERMLINE'`
- **Somatic:** `upper(mutation_status) = 'SOMATIC'` — but only when the user asks for somatic-only. Many studies label their somatic calls `'NA'` or `'UNKNOWN'`, so for ordinary mutation questions follow common-pitfalls #3 and exclude only `'UNCALLED'`.

# Common Query Pitfalls Guide

## Overview
This guide highlights frequent mistakes when analyzing cBioPortal data and provides solutions to avoid them.

## Critical Pitfalls

### 1. 🚨 CRITICAL MUTATION FREQUENCY ERRORS

#### ❌ WRONG: Using study-wide totals for gene frequencies
```sql
-- INCORRECT - This gives wrong frequencies!
SELECT
    hugo_gene_symbol,
    COUNT(DISTINCT sample_unique_id) as altered_samples,
    (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT sample_unique_id)
     FROM genomic_event_derived
     WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id') as total_samples
FROM genomic_event_derived
WHERE variant_type = 'mutation' AND cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY hugo_gene_symbol;
```
**Problem**: Different genes have different profiling coverage - you can't use study-wide totals!

#### ❌ WRONG: Not using gene-specific profiling denominators
```sql
-- INCORRECT - Missing gene-specific denominators
```

reply.answer:
## Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma (salivary gland): Expected Drivers

Using the largest ACC/ACYC pan-cohort in cBioPortal — [Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma Project (J Clin Invest 2019)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acc_2019), 1,049 samples — here is the alteration landscape (all frequencies = altered / profiled samples; **patient-level data not separately available, counts are sample-level**; cBioPortal does not store an OncoKB/driver annotation flag for this study, so nothing below should be read as "confirmed oncogenic" unless independently verified in the literature):

### Structural Variants / Fusions — the defining lesion
| Gene | Altered / Profiled | % |
|---|---|---|
| MYB | 187/1049 | 17.8% |
| NFIB | 173/1049 | 16.5% |

The hallmark event in ACC is the **t(6;9) MYB-NFIB fusion** (and related MYB/MYBL1 rearrangements) — present in roughly one-third of tumors combined, driving overexpression of the MYB transcription factor oncogene.

### Most Frequently Mutated Genes (point mutations/indels)
| Gene | Altered / Profiled | % | Functional class |
|---|---|---|---|
| NOTCH1 | 232/1049 | 22.1% | Tumor suppressor (truncating) / oncogene (activating) — context-dependent |
| KDM6A | 138/1049 | 13.2% | Chromatin modifier (tumor suppressor) |
| ARID1A | 120/1049 | 11.4% | SWI/SNF chromatin remodeler (tumor suppressor) |
| KMT2D | 111/1049 | 10.6% | Chromatin modifier (tumor suppressor) |
| **BCOR** | **109/1049** | **10.4%** | Chromatin/transcriptional corepressor (tumor suppressor) |
| KMT2C | 99/1049 | 9.4% | Chromatin modifier |
| CREBBP | 98/1049 | 9.3% | Histone acetyltransferase |
| ARID1B | 82/1049 | 7.8% | SWI/SNF chromatin remodeler |
| TERT | 82/1049 | 7.8% | Telomerase (often promoter) |
| TP53 | 76/1049 | 7.2% | Tumor suppressor |

### Copy Number / Amplifications
PDGFRA (3.9%), KIT (3.3%), KDR (3.1%) — co-amplified as part of the 4q12 amplicon; MDM2 (2.7%, 12q15); CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion (~3%).

---

## Classification by Actionability

**Tier 1 — Clinically actionable (targeted therapy context exists)**
- **MYB-NFIB fusion** — the core ACC lesion; drives transcriptional dysregulation. Not directly druggable itself, but downstream pathway targeting (e.g., Notch inhibitors, given MYB's transactivation of NOTCH1) is under clinical investigation.
- **NOTCH1** (activating mutations) — Notch pathway inhibitors (gamma-secretase inhibitors, e.g., AL101/crenigacestat) have been studied specifically in NOTCH-activated ACC in trials.
- **KIT/PDGFRA amplification** — potential rationale for tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib, sunitinib), though clinical responses in ACC have historically been modest/inconsistent.
- **NTRK1** rearrangement/alteration (3.8% in this cohort) — TRK inhibitors (larotrectinib, entrectinib) are tissue-agnostic approved therapies when a fusion is confirmed.
- **MDM2 amplification** — rationale for MDM2 inhibitors (investigational), contingent on functional TP53.

**Tier 2 — Potentially actionable / investigational**
- **TERT** (promoter) — no direct inhibitor approved; prognostic/biomarker relevance only at present.
- **CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion** — rationale for CDK4/6 inhibitors (investigational in this context).
- **FGFR1** and other RTK alterations — pathway inhibitors exist but gene-specific activating events are uncommon in this cohort.

**Tier 3 — Not currently actionable (prognostic/structural only)**
- **BCOR, KDM6A, ARID1A, ARID1B, KMT2D, KMT2C, CREBBP** — predominantly truncating loss-of-function mutations in chromatin-modifying/SWI-SNF genes. No approved targeted therapy exists for loss-of-function in these genes; they are tumor-suppressor-pattern events of likely biological importance (epigenetic dysregulation) but not direct drug targets today.
- **TP53** — loss-of-function, not directly druggable with approved agents.

---

## BCOR Specifically

- **Frequency:** 109/1049 samples (10.4%) in `acc_2019` — the **5th most frequently mutated gene** in this cohort, so it is a recurrent and notable (not incidental) finding in ACC.
- **Mutation pattern:** Overwhelmingly **truncating** — nonsense mutations, frameshift insertions/deletions, and a splice-site variant scattered across the gene body (e.g., E983\*, Q600Hfs\*11, S1297\*, L279Rfs\*21), with only a minority of missense changes. This pattern is classic for **loss-of-function of a tumor suppressor** rather than a hotspot/gain-of-function oncogene.
- **Somatic vs. germline — direct answer to your question:** I checked `mutation_status` for BCOR across **all seven** ACC/ACYC studies in the database (acc_2019, acyc_mda_2015, acyc_mskcc_2013, acyc_fmi_2014, acyc_jhu_2016, acyc_sanger_2013, acyc_mgh_2016). **Every single BCOR mutation record is annotated SOMATIC. There are zero germline BCOR mutations recorded in any ACC/ACYC study in cBioPortal** (and in fact zero germline mutation calls of any gene across all these ACC cohorts — none of these seven studies loaded germline variant data at all). I cannot speak to germline BCOR variants in ACC from literature outside this database; if you're asking because of a specific patient with a germline BCOR finding (e.g., BCOR internal tandem duplication syndrome, a distinct pediatric entity), that would need to be evaluated independently — it is not represented in this dataset.
- No OncoKB/driver-annotation flag is loaded for `acc_2019`, so I cannot label BCOR mutations here as "confirmed oncogenic drivers" from the database alone — only as recurrently and predominantly truncating, consistent with tumor-suppressor inactivation.

### Links
- **[OncoPrint — drivers panel](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/oncoprint?cancer_study_list=acc_2019&gene_list=MYB%0ANFIB%0ANOTCH1%0ABCOR%0AKDM6A%0AARID1A%0AKMT2D%0ATP53%0AFGFR1%0ASMO%0AKIT%0APDGFRA%0AMDM2%0ACDKN2A%0ANTRK1&case_set_id=acc_2019_all)** — co-occurrence pattern of the genes above across the 1,049-sample cohort.
- **[Study View filtered to BCOR-mutant samples](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acc_2019#filterJson=%7B%22geneFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22geneQueries%22%3A%5B%5B%7B%22hugoGeneSymbol%22%3A%22BCOR%22%7D%5D%5D%2C%22molecularProfileIds%22%3A%5B%22acc_2019_mutations%22%5D%7D%5D%7D)** — clinical/demographic breakdown of BCOR-mutant cases.

Note: smaller companion ACC cohorts also exist in cBioPortal ([MSK 2013](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acyc_mskcc_2013), [MDA 2015](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acyc_mda_2015), [FMI 2014](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acyc_fmi_2014), [JHU 2016](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acyc_jhu_2016), [Sanger/MDA 2013](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acyc_sanger_2013), [MGH 2016](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=acyc_mgh_2016)) — all were checked and show the same 100%-somatic BCOR pattern, just with smaller sample sizes.

tool_calls.result:
# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

## Counting Unit: Samples vs Patients

Before answering any mutation count or frequency question, decide whether the unit is samples or patients and state that choice in the answer.

======================

Overview
--------
cBioPortal stores both somatic AND germline variant data. Many cBioPortal features work identically for both variant types. This guide explains how to query germline variants and what to be aware of.

```python
"""
Query MSK-CHORD Timeline/Clinical Events Data

This module provides utilities for querying clinical timeline events
from the MSK-CHORD cohort in cBioPortal.
"""

import requests
import pandas as pd
from typing import List, Dict, Optional, Tuple
import json


class MSKChordTimelineQuerier:
    """Query clinical timeline/event data from MSK-CHORD study."""
    
    # API endpoints
    REST_API_BASE = "https://www.cbioportal.org/api"
    STUDY_ID = "msk_chord_2024"
    
    def __init__(self):
        """Initialize the querier with study-specific constants."""
        self.study_id = self.STUDY_ID
        self.session = requests.Session()
    
    # ============================================================================
    # SECTION 1: Clinical Events (Timeline Data) - REST API
    # ============================================================================
    
    def get_patient_timeline_events(
        self,
        patient_id: str,
        event_type: Optional[str] = None
    ) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """
        Fetch all timeline events for a single patient.
        
        Args:
            patient_id: Patient identifier (e.g., "[patient id]")
            event_type: Optional filter (e.g., "TREATMENT", "Diagnosis", "Progression")
                       If None, returns all event types.
        
        Returns:
            DataFrame with columns: event_type, start_date, stop_date, and event-specific attributes
        
        Example:
            >>> querier = MSKChordTimelineQuerier()
            >>> events = querier.get_patient_timeline_events("[patient id]")
            >>> treatment_events = querier.get_patient_timeline_events("[patient id]", event_type="TREATMENT")
        """
        endpoint = f"{self.REST_API_BASE}/studies/{self.study_id}/patients/{patient_id}/timeline-events"
        
        try:
            response = self.session.get(endpoint, timeout=30)
            response.raise_for_status()
            events = response.json()
            
            # Filter by event type if specified
            if event_type:
                events = [e for e in events if e.get('eventType') == event_type]
            
            # Convert to DataFrame for easier analysis
            if events:
                df = pd.json_normalize(events)
                return df.sort_values('startNumberOfDaysSinceDiagnosis', na_position='last')
            else:
                return pd.DataFrame()
        
        except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
            print(f"Error fetching timeline for patient {patient_id}: {e}")
            return pd.DataFrame()
    
    def get_all_patients_timelines(
        self,
        event_type: Optional[str] = None,
        cancer_type: Optional[str] = None,
        sample_type: Optional[str] = None
    ) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """
        Fetch timeline events for all patients in MSK-CHORD.
        
        Args:
            event_type: Optional filter (e.g., "TREATMENT", "Diagnosis")
            cancer_type: Optional cancer type filter (e.g., "Lung Adenocarcinoma")
            sample_type: Optional sample type filter (e.g., "Primary", "Metastasis")
        
        Returns:
            DataFrame aggregating events from all patients
        
        Note:
            This makes one API call per patient (~25k calls) - use cautiously
            or batch with parameter filters for efficiency.
        """
        # First get all patients
        patients = self.get_all_patients()
        
        all_events = []
        for idx, patient_id in enumerate(patients, 1):
            if idx % 1000 == 0:
                print(f"Processing patient {idx}/{len(patients)}...")
            
            events_df = self.get_patient_timeline_events(patient_id, event_type)
            if not events_df.empty:
                events_df['patientId'] = patient_id
                all_events.append(events_df)
        
        if all_events:
            return pd.concat(all_events, ignore_index=True)
        else:
            return pd.DataFrame()
    
    def get_all_patients(self) -> List[str]:
        """Get list of all patient IDs in MSK-CHORD study."""
        endpoint = f"{self.REST_API_BASE}/studies/{self.study_id}/patients"
        
        try:
            response = self.session.get(endpoint, timeout=30)
            response.raise_for_status()
            patients = response.json()
            return [p['patientId'] for p in patients]
        except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
            print(f"Error fetching patient list: {e}")
            return []
    
    # ============================================================================
    # SECTION 2: Treatment Events - ClickHouse Direct Query
    # ============================================================================
    
    def query_treatments_via_sql(
        self,
        include_fields: Optional[List[str]] = None
    ) -> str:
        """
        Generate a ClickHouse SQL query for treatment events.
        
        Args:
            include_fields: List of event data keys to include (e.g., ['AGENT', 'SUBTYPE', 'START_DATE'])
        
        Returns:
            SQL query string ready to execute
        
        Example:
            >>> sql = querier.query_treatments_via_sql(['AGENT', 'SUBTYPE'])
            >>> # Execute this in ClickHouse or via cBioPortal backend
        """
        if include_fields is None:
            include_fields = ['AGENT', 'SUBTYPE', 'START_DATE', 'STOP_DATE']
        
        sql = f"""
        SELECT 
            ce.patient_stable_id,
            ce.event_type,
            ce.start_date,
            ce.stop_date,
            arrayMap(
                (k, v) -> CONCAT(k, '=', v),
                groupArray(ced.key),
                groupArray(ced.value)
            ) as event_attributes,
            -- Extract specific fields
            {self._generate_pivot_columns(include_fields)}
        FROM clinical_event_derived ce
        LEFT JOIN clinical_event_data_derived ced USING (clinical_event_id)
        WHERE ce.cancer_study_identifier = '{self.study_id}'
            AND ce.event_type IN ('TREATMENT', 'Treatment')

        ORDER BY ce.patient_stable_id, ce.start_date

        """
        return sql

        """

            ce.event_type,
            ce.start_date,
            ced.key,
            ced.value
        FROM clinical_event_derived ce
        LEFT JOIN clinical_event_data_derived ced USING (clinical_event_id)
        WHERE ce.cancer_study_identifier = '{self.study_id}'
            AND ce.event_type IN ('DIAGNOSIS', 'Diagnosis')
        ORDER BY ce.patient_stable_id, ce.start_date;
        """
        return sql
    
    def query_progressions_via_sql(self) -> str:
        """
        Generate SQL query for progression events.
        
        Returns:
            SQL query string
        """
        sql = f"""
        SELECT 
            ce.patient_stable_id,
            ce.event_type,
            ce.start_date,
            ced.key,
            ced.value
        FROM clinical_event_derived ce
        LEFT JOIN clinical_event_data_derived ced USING (clinical_event_id)
        WHERE ce.cancer_study_identifier = '{self.study_id}'
            AND ce.event_type IN ('PROGRESSION', 'Progression')
            AND ced.key = 'PROGRESSION'
            AND ced.value IN ('Y', 'Indeterminate')
        ORDER BY ce.patient_stable_id, ce.start_date;
        """
        return sql
    
    def query_patient_treatment_timeline(self, patient_id: str) -> str:
        """
        Generate SQL query for a single patient's treatment timeline.
        
        Args:
            patient_id: Patient stable ID (e.g., "[patient id]")
        
        Returns:
            SQL query string
        """
        sql = f"""
        SELECT 
            ce.patient_stable_id,
            ce.start_date,
            ce.stop_date,
            ce.event_type,
            ced.key,
            ced.value
        FROM clinical_event_derived ce
        LEFT JOIN clinical_event_data_derived ced USING (clinical_event_id)
        WHERE ce.cancer_study_identifier = '{self.study_id}'
            AND ce.patient_stable_id = '{patient_id}'
            AND ce.event_type IN ('TREATMENT', 'Treatment')
        ORDER BY ce.start_date ASC;
        """
        return sql
    
    def query_timeline_summary_by_cancer_type(self) -> str:
        """
        Generate SQL query summarizing event types by cancer type.
        
        Returns:
            SQL query string
        """
        sql = f"""
        SELECT 
            ccd.attribute_value as cancer_type,
            ce.event_type,
            COUNT(DISTINCT ce.patient_stable_id) as patient_count,
            COUNT(DISTINCT ce.clinical_event_id) as event_count
        FROM clinical_event_derived ce
        LEFT JOIN clinical_data_derived ccd ON (
            ce.patient_id = ccd.patient_id 
            AND ccd.cancer_study_identifier = ce.cancer_study_identifier
            AND ccd.attribute_name = 'CANCER_TYPE'
        )
        WHERE ce.cancer_study_identifier = '{self.study_id}'
        GROUP BY cancer_type, ce.event_type
        ORDER BY cancer_type, patient_count DESC;
        """
        return sql

    @staticmethod
    def _generate_pivot_columns(fields: List[str]) -> str:
        """Generate SQL CASE statements to extract specific event data fields."""
        cases = []
        for field in fields:
            cases.append(f"""
            arrayStringConcat(
                arrayFilter(v -> startsWith(v, '{field}='), 
                arrayMap((k, v) -> CONCAT(k, '=', v), groupArray(ced.key), groupArray(ced.value))),
                ', '
            ) as {field}
            """)
        return ", ".join(cases)
    
    def get_event_type_counts(self) -> Dict[str, int]:
        """
        Return counts of each event type in the study.
        
        Returns:
            Dictionary mapping event_type to count
        """
        sql = f"""
        SELECT event_type, COUNT(*) as count
        FROM clinical_event_derived
        WHERE cancer_study_identifier = '{self.study_id}'
        GROUP BY event_type;
```

   - `get_patient_timeline_events()` — fetch timeline for one patient

reply.answer:
Here's Python code using the public cBioPortal REST API to query timeline (clinical event) data for the MSK-CHORD 2024 study (`msk_chord_2024`). This retrieves per-patient clinical timeline events (treatments, diagnoses, surgeries, sample acquisitions, etc. — the same events that back the Patient View timeline).

```python
"""
Query timeline / clinical event data for MSK-CHORD (msk_chord_2024)
from the public cBioPortal REST API.

Docs: https://www.cbioportal.org/api/swagger-ui/index.html
"""

import requests
import pandas as pd

BASE_URL = "https://www.cbioportal.org/api"
STUDY_ID = "msk_chord_2024"


def get_all_patient_ids(study_id: str) -> list[str]:
    """Fetch all patient IDs in the study."""
    resp = requests.get(
        f"{BASE_URL}/studies/{study_id}/patients",
        params={"projection": "ID"},
    )
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return [p["patientId"] for p in resp.json()]


def get_clinical_events(study_id: str, patient_ids: list[str],
                         batch_size: int = 500) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """
    Fetch clinical timeline events for a list of patients, in batches.

    Each event has: patientId, startDate, stopDate, eventType,
    and a nested list of key/value attributes (e.g. AGENT, SUBTYPE for
    Treatment events).
    """
    all_rows = []

    for i in range(0, len(patient_ids), batch_size):
        batch = patient_ids[i:i + batch_size]
        resp = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/studies/{study_id}/clinical-events/fetch",
            params={"projection": "DETAILED"},
            json={"ids": batch},
        )
        resp.raise_for_status()
        events = resp.json()

        for ev in events:
            row = {
                "patientId": ev.get("patientId"),
                "eventType": ev.get("eventType"),
                "startDate": ev.get("startDate"),
                "stopDate": ev.get("stopDate"),
            }
            # Flatten key/value attributes (e.g. AGENT, SUBTYPE, PROGRESSION)
            for attr in ev.get("attributes", []):
                row[attr["key"]] = attr["value"]
            all_rows.append(row)

    return pd.DataFrame(all_rows)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    patient_ids = get_all_patient_ids(STUDY_ID)
    print(f"Found {len(patient_ids)} patients in {STUDY_ID}")

    # For a quick test, limit to a small subset before pulling the full cohort
    # (25k patients' full timelines is a large payload)
    sample_ids = patient_ids[:50]
    df = get_clinical_events(STUDY_ID, sample_ids)

    print(df["eventType"].value_counts())
    print(df.head(20))

    # Example: isolate Treatment events and show top agents
    treatments = df[df["eventType"].str.upper() == "TREATMENT"]
    if "AGENT" in treatments.columns:
        print(treatments["AGENT"].value_counts().head(10))

    # Save full results to CSV
    df.to_csv("msk_chord_2024_clinical_events.csv", index=False)
```

**Notes specific to this study:**
- Event types you'll encounter: `Treatment`, `Diagnosis`, `Sample acquisition`, `Surgery`, `Lab_test`, `Pathology`, among others.
- Treatment events carry `AGENT` (drug name) and `SUBTYPE` (Chemo, Immuno, Targeted, Hormone, Radiation Therapy, etc.) as key/value attributes.
- `startDate`/`stopDate` are in days relative to a reference point (not calendar dates), consistent with how the Patient View timeline renders them.
- MSK-CHORD has ~24,950 patients — pulling the full cohort's timeline in one call is a large payload, so the code batches requests (POST `/clinical-events/fetch` is the batchable endpoint; the single-patient GET `/patients/{patientId}/clinical-events` also works for one-off lookups).
- This data is under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license (contact [email redacted] for commercial use).

If you'd like, I can also open the live timeline for a specific patient in the portal — just give me a patient or sample ID. You can also browse the cohort directly here: [MSK-CHORD Study View](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=msk_chord_2024).

Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

# Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

### 4. Find Studies by Available Data Types

Use this when the user asks *"which studies have mutation and copy-number data for X"*, *"studies with expression for Y"*, *"is there any imaging data"*, or any *"studies with Z data"* question. `cancer_study` has one precomputed sample count per data type — filter on them. reply.answer:
The database contains a wide range of cancers from diverse sources including TCGA, MSK, pediatric studies (TARGET), and others. Here's a summary of the major cancer types represented:

## Major Cancer Types

**Solid Tumors:**
- **Lung:** Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)
- **Breast:** Invasive breast carcinoma, metastatic breast cancer
- **Colorectal:** Colorectal/colon/rectal adenocarcinoma
- **Ovarian:** High-grade serous ovarian cancer
- **Endometrial:** Uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma
- **Prostate:** Prostate adenocarcinoma
- **Pancreatic:** Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)
- **Kidney:** Renal clear cell carcinoma (CCRCC)
- **Hepatic:** Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)
- **Biliary:** Hepatobiliary/biliary tract cancer
- **Esophageal/Gastric:** Esophagogastric cancer
- **Bladder:** Urothelial bladder cancer
- **Melanoma:** Cutaneous melanoma (SKCM)
- **Sarcoma:** Soft tissue and bone sarcomas
- **Glioma:** Diffuse gliomas, glioblastoma

**Hematologic Malignancies:**
- **Leukemias:** Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoid leukemia (ALL/BLL)
- **Lymphomas:** Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)
- **Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS)**
- **Other heme:** Histiocytic and dendritic cell neoplasms, mature B-cell malignancies

**Other Types:**
- **Pediatric cancers** across multiple types (neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, etc.)
- **Adenoid cystic carcinoma**
- **Mixed/pan-cancer cohorts** (cross-study panels like MSK-IMPACT, MSK-CHORD)

## Data Sources
- **TCGA:** Includes legacy and Pan-Cancer Atlas versions
- **MSK:** Major MSK institutional cohorts (MSK-IMPACT, MSK-CHORD, MSK-ACCESS)
- **TARGET GDC:** Pediatric cancer consortium
- **Other sources:** Broad Institute (CCLE), ICGC/PCAWG, institutional centers (OHSU, St. Jude, MD Anderson), and international studies

The largest cohorts are **pan-cancer** (mixed tumor types) like MSK-IMPACT 50K (54k samples) and MSK-CHORD (25k samples). For disease-specific studies, you can browse at [cBioPortal](https://www.cbioportal.org) or search for a specific cancer type or institution here.

The database contains **122 distinct cancer types** spanning **531 studies**, organized across roughly 30 tissue categories. Highlights:

**Most-studied cancer types (by number of studies):**
| Cancer type | Tissue | Studies |
|---|---|---|
| Mixed Cancer Types (pan-cancer cohorts, e.g. MSK-IMPACT, MSK-CHORD) | Other | 48 |
| Invasive Breast Carcinoma | Breast | 27 |
| Prostate Adenocarcinoma | Prostate | 25 |
| Diffuse Glioma | CNS/Brain | 20 |
| Bladder Urothelial Carcinoma | Bladder/Urinary Tract | 18 |
| Lung Adenocarcinoma | Lung | 17 |
| Colorectal Adenocarcinoma | Bowel | 16 |
| Soft Tissue Sarcomas (general) | Soft Tissue | 13 |
| Hepatocellular Carcinoma | Liver | 12 |
| Cutaneous Melanoma | Skin | 12 |
| Endometrial Carcinoma | Uterus | 12 |

**Broad tissue coverage includes:** Breast, Prostate, CNS/Brain, Lung, Bladder/Urinary Tract, Bowel, Liver, Skin, Uterus, Kidney, Pancreas, Esophagus/Stomach, Head & Neck, Myeloid & Lymphoid malignancies (leukemias/lymphomas), Ovary/Fallopian Tube, Soft Tissue & Bone sarcomas, Thyroid, Adrenal Gland, Testis, Cervix, Thymus, Eye (melanoma/retinoblastoma), Pleura, Biliary Tract, and several rarer entities (e.g., ampullary carcinoma, schwannoma, appendiceal adenocarcinoma).

Note: "Mixed Cancer Types" studies are multi-cancer cohorts (like large clinical sequencing panels); their individual samples are annotated with specific cancer types internally rather than being one single entity.

## What is cBioPortal?

cBioPortal for Cancer Genomics is an open-access, open-source resource for interactive exploration of multidimensional cancer genomics data sets. It was originally developed at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) and is now maintained by a multi-institutional team.

## History

- **2008**: cBioPortal first became available online.
- **2012**: First major publication — Cerami et al., *Cancer Discovery*.
- **2013**: Second major publication — Gao et al., *Science Signaling*.

reply.answer:
The cBioPortal database backend doesn't directly track the raw data files (like `data_clinical_outcomes.txt`). However, I can guide you to find studies with outcome data that you can emulate:

## Studies with Clinical Outcome Data

Based on the studies in the database, several large cohorts have rich clinical outcome data. Here are some good candidates to reference:

### **Recommended Studies to Emulate:**

1. **[MSK-CHORD (MSK, Nature 2024)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=msk_chord_2024)** — 25,040 tumors
   - Pan-cancer clinical sequencing with extensive clinical annotations
   - Has a pre-generated study guide available
   - Includes survival and treatment data

2. **[MSK-IMPACT Clinical Sequencing Cohort (MSK, Nat Med 2017)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=msk_impact_2017)** — 10,945 samples
   - Well-established format; good reference for MSK data standards

3. **[TMB and Immunotherapy (MSK, Nat Genet 2019)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=tmb_mskcc_2018)** — 1,661 samples
   - Specifically includes survival data (OS outcomes)

4. **[Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS IWG, IPSSM, NEJM Evidence 2022)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=mds_iwg_2022)** — 3,323 samples
   - Disease-specific with comprehensive prognostic outcome data

## How to Access the Raw Files

The actual `data_clinical_outcomes.txt` and associated metadata files are in the **cBioPortal Data Hub** on GitHub:

📁 **GitHub Location:** https://github.com/cbioportal/datahub/tree/master/public

For example:
- MSK-CHORD: `https://github.com/cbioportal/datahub/tree/master/public/msk_chord_2024`
- MSK-IMPACT 2017: `https://github.com/cbioportal/datahub/tree/master/public/msk_impact_2017`

Each study folder contains:
- `data_clinical_outcomes.txt` — patient outcome data
- `meta_clinical_outcomes.txt` — metadata/schema file
- `data_clinical_patient.txt` — patient demographics
- `data_clinical_sample.txt` — sample-level annotations

## Next Steps

1. **Browse the datahub** for a study matching your tumor type and data richness
2. **Copy the meta file** as your template (defines column names, data types, descriptions)
3. **Use the data file format** to structure your own outcome data

Would you like me to help you query a specific study to understand what outcome variables they track, or do you need guidance on the meta file format itself?

The notation **p.*1069Wext*3** is an unconventional or typographical variant — it doesn't match standard cBioPortal nomenclature for PIK3CA mutations. Let me clarify what you may be seeing:

1. **Interpretation of the notation:**
   - The `p.*` prefix indicates a protein-level notation (HGVS nomenclature)
   - The `*1069` likely refers to a **stop codon** position (in HGVS, `*` after the position means downstream of the normal stop codon)
   - `Wext*3` is **unusual** — this looks like it could be:
     - A **typo** for a known PIK3CA hotspot (e.g., **H1047R**, **E542K**, **E545K**, **E546K**)
     - An annotation from a specialist annotation tool (e.g., a clinical report using non-standard nomenclature)
     - A **nonsense or extended-stop mutation** (though the format is atypical)

2. **What cBioPortal stores:**
   - PIK3CA is one of the most frequently mutated genes across cancers (especially breast, ovarian, uterine, endometrial)
   - Common PIK3CA hotspots in cBioPortal are: **H1047R** (helical domain), **E542K**, **E545K** (kinase domain) — these account for ~80% of PIK3CA mutations
   - cBioPortal normalizes variant notation but does **not** store every possible synonymous notation variant

3. **How to proceed:**
   - **Check your source report:** Does it specify the actual nucleotide change (e.g., chr3:179234297 C>T) or a protein change that's more standard? 
   - **Is this a truncating mutation?** If the report states the mutation is a **stop codon extension** or **nonsense**, that's a distinct functional class from activating hotspots.

# Gene Resolution Guide

Use this guide before querying gene expression, mutation, copy-number, methylation, or structural-variant data when the user's gene term may be ambiguous.

## Routing Triggers

Read this guide when the user mentions:

- a gene family shorthand: `CD3`, `HLA`, `KRT`, `MUC`, `MT-`, `IGH`, `IGK`, `IGL`
- a marker name that may refer to multiple genes or proteins
- a gene alias, old symbol, or informal name
- a wildcard-like term such as "all CD3 genes"

These examples are not exhaustive. Apply this guide to any gene term that may resolve to multiple symbols, aliases, paralogs, family members, or marker genes.

## Core Rule

Do not silently aggregate multiple genes when the user names an ambiguous symbol. Either ask for clarification or choose a clearly standard marker and state the choice.

For example, "CD3 expression" can refer to `CD3D`, `CD3E`, or `CD3G`; in many immune-marker contexts `CD3E` is the standard marker, but the agent must not average all CD3 genes unless the user asks for a combined signature.

```sql
FROM gene
WHERE upper(hugo_gene_symbol) = upper('CD3')

LIMIT 50;
```

question.question: Can you explore the difference in mutation frequency between left-sided and right-sided CRC?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: explain that left vs right sidedness is defined by the splenic flexure (not colon vs rectum), use sub-site annotations where a study has them, or say the data doesn't support the comparison.
Must not: substitute a colon-vs-rectum comparison.

reply.answer:
## Mutation Frequency Differences: Left-Sided vs Right-Sided CRC

I've analyzed the **MSK Colorectal Adenocarcinoma 2026 study** (7,237 samples, 744 right-sided + 1,159 left-sided cases) and found striking differences in mutation patterns:

### **Key Findings:**

#### **Right-Sided CRC is Characterized by:**
- **BRAF mutations** — 24.9% (right) vs 7.7% (left), **+17.2 percentage points**
- **RNF43 mutations** — 24.3% (right) vs 5.3% (left), **+19 percentage points**
- **KRAS mutations** — 54% (right) vs 35.5% (left), **+18.5 percentage points**
- **Mismatch repair genes** (MSH3, MSH6, MLH1, POLD1) — consistently 3–5× higher
- **PIK3CA mutations** — 32.8% (right) vs 16.6% (left), **+16.2 percentage points**

#### **Left-Sided CRC is Characterized by:**
- **TP53 mutations** — 80.2% (left) vs 57.3% (right), **−22.9 percentage points**
- **APC mutations** — 79.9% (left) vs 64.8% (right), **−15.1 percentage points**
- Slightly higher FBXW7 mutations (12% left vs 17.1% right)

#### **Interpretation:**
Right-sided tumors show enrichment for:
- **Serrated pathway features** (BRAF, RNF43, PIK3CA mutations)
- **Microsatellite instability (MSI)** markers (MSH2/6, MLH1 mutations)
- **CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP)** genotype

Left-sided tumors show:
- Classic chromosomal instability (CIN) features
- Higher TP53 and APC mutations (adenoma-carcinoma sequence)

---

### **Interactive Exploration:**

**[View Right-Sided CRC (744 samples)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=crc_msk_2026&filterAttributeId=PRIMARY_SITE&filterValues=Cecum%2CAscending+Colon%2CAscending+colon%2CHepatic+Flexure%2CHepatic+flexure)** — Cecum, ascending colon, hepatic flexure

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
